claims.text: A thin, controlled oxide overlayer on platinum-group nanoscale catalysts alters the surface electronic structure.
The altered electronic structure facilitates ethanol oxidation by enhancing intermediate desorption and reducing catalyst poisoning.
Complete ethanol oxidation involves transfer of 12 electrons and 12 protons.
The proposed initial state is a clean, metallic PGM nanoparticle surface lacking a significant oxide layer.
Selective pre-oxidation can generate a controlled sub-monolayer oxide on the PGM catalyst surface.
A 0.5 M sulfuric-acid electrolyte at 60–80 °C is representative of electrochemical fuel-cell ethanol-oxidation conditions.
The sub-monolayer oxide enhances adsorption and desorption kinetics of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The sub-monolayer oxide promotes favorable water activation.
The sub-monolayer oxide suppresses poisoning by carbonaceous species.
Suppressing poisoning and improving intermediate kinetics increase ethanol-oxidation activity, selectivity, and durability.
Oxide-treated catalysts will exhibit higher ethanol-oxidation current density than untreated metallic catalysts.
Oxide-treated catalysts will show greater selectivity toward complete ethanol-oxidation products than untreated metallic catalysts.
Oxide-treated catalysts will be more durable than untreated metallic catalysts.
Untreated metallic PGM surfaces are less effective at mediating the electron–proton transfer steps of ethanol oxidation.
The beneficial catalytic effect occurs only when oxide coverage remains thin and sub-monolayer.
Oxide coverage above a critical threshold creates a thick, insulating layer that decreases catalytic activity.
The exact beneficial oxide thickness and its electronic effect on active sites are not quantitatively defined.
